title: The top cities in Central Asia and the South Caucasus in 2026
gist: Oxford Economics' 2026 Global Cities Index view of Central Asia and the South Caucasus (byline in text: Swayam Tanna; raw author field: Sally Li): 10 major cities are forecast to grow 4.1%/yr over 25 years vs 2.7% for Asia-Pacific cities, led by Tashkent (6.2%/yr, set to overtake Almaty) and Bishkek, powered by young, skilled, fast-growing populations and the Middle Corridor trade role, but held back by weak Governance and Environment scores.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics forecasts real GDP across 10 of the largest Central Asia and South Caucasus city economies to grow 4.1% a year over the next 25 years, versus 2.7% for Asia Pacific's cities, with combined city GDP over 2.5 times today's by 2050.
insights.speaker: Swayam Tanna
insights.so_what: Positions the region as a long-duration frontier growth play for FDI, consumer and infrastructure exposure.

insights.claim: Tashkent and Bishkek both rank among the top 10 fastest-growing of the 1,000 cities in Oxford Economics' 2026 Global Cities Index.
insights.speaker: Swayam Tanna
insights.so_what: Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan urban centers are where growth is most concentrated.

insights.claim: The region's growing role as a China–Europe trade route, notably the Middle Corridor, underpins its urban growth prospects.
insights.speaker: Swayam Tanna
insights.so_what: Logistics, transit infrastructure and trade-finance in the region benefit from rerouted Eurasian trade.
insights.locator: But with the region taking on a growing role

insights.claim: Human Capital is the strongest Global Cities Index category for eight of 10 Central Asia/South Caucasus cities, with Almaty (66th), Astana (98th), Tashkent (108th) and Ashgabat (146th) in the global top 150.
insights.speaker: Swayam Tanna
insights.so_what: Skilled, relatively cheap labor supports nearshoring of services and IT to the region.

insights.claim: Kazakhstan now hosts more than 30 foreign university branches, including Cardiff University's Astana campus, while Baku's and Almaty's universities rank 57th and 67th globally and Tbilisi ranks 36th for adult mean years of schooling.
insights.speaker: Swayam Tanna
insights.so_what: Deliberate talent-pool building strengthens Kazakhstan's case as a regional services hub.

insights.claim: Astana, Almaty, Dushanbe and Bishkek rank in the top 10% of cities globally for population growth, with Astana's population set to double by 2050 and the region's major cities adding more than 8 million residents over 25 years, while Yerevan's population is forecast to decline.
insights.speaker: Swayam Tanna
insights.so_what: Demographic tailwinds favor Central Asian over South Caucasus cities for consumer and housing demand.

insights.claim: Employment growth in Dushanbe (23rd) and Astana (25th) ranks in the global top 25 and, combined with rising productivity, is expected to drive rising incomes and consumer appetite.
insights.speaker: Swayam Tanna
insights.so_what: Growing consumer markets for retail, banking and telecom in Central Asia.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics expects Tashkent's economy to grow 6.2% a year over 25 years, the seventh-fastest of any city globally, overtaking Almaty as the region's largest city economy within a few years and outgrowing Rome and Vienna by 2050.
insights.speaker: Swayam Tanna
insights.so_what: Uzbekistan is the region's standout growth story — relevant for frontier equity/debt and FDI allocation.

insights.claim: Tashkent's momentum stems from Uzbekistan's economic liberalisation and opening, the Tashkent IT Park, the 'New Tashkent' construction megaproject and its position on the Middle Corridor trade route.
insights.speaker: Swayam Tanna
insights.so_what: Construction, tech services and logistics are the sectors riding Uzbekistan's reform cycle.

insights.claim: Tashkent's productivity is forecast to almost triple by 2050, but low incomes risk talent emigration, and Uzbekistan relies on external sources for 80% of its water, alongside high housing costs.
insights.speaker: Swayam Tanna
insights.so_what: Water dependence is a material physical/geopolitical risk to the Uzbek growth thesis.
insights.quote: with Uzbekistan relying on external sources for 80% of its water

insights.claim: All 10 major Central Asia and South Caucasus cities rank outside the global top 500 for civil liberties and top 600 for temperature anomalies, with emissions intensity and poor air quality weighing on Tashkent, Ashgabat and Dushanbe.
insights.speaker: Swayam Tanna
insights.so_what: Governance and environmental risk are the key discounts investors must price against the region's growth.
